Detailed entries for `QPKG-001..QPKG-007`. Each follows the four-part
**What / Why / How / When NOT to apply** shape. "QDK guide" means
`docs/QDK-Developer-Guide.md` in [qnap-dev/QDK](https://github.com/qnap-dev/QDK)
(QDK 2.5.3, 2026-09).

---

## QPKG-001 — Choose a native QPKG or a Container Station app on purpose

**What.** Before writing a QPKG, decide whether the app would be better as a
Container Station (Docker / `docker compose`) app. Build a native QPKG only
when it buys something a container cannot: tight integration with QTS (App
Center lifecycle, the QTS web proxy, Resource Monitor), a small RAM and disk
footprint, or a model where Container Station is unavailable.

**Why.** A native package owns problems a container image solves for you: a
static build per CPU architecture (QPKG-008), the boot-time root filesystem
reset (QPKG-015), upgrade-safe config (QPKG-022) and code-signing friction
(QPKG-034). An upstream that already publishes an official multi-arch image
gets upgrades with a tag change. Containers share the host kernel, so a
kernel page-size limit (QPKG-009) still applies inside them.

**How.** A container version for comparison:

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml in Container Station (QTS ships `docker compose`, v2)
services:
  app:
    image: example/app:1.4.2
    ports: ["9100:9000"]
    volumes: ["/share/AppData/app:/data"]
    restart: unless-stopped
```

Prefer the native QPKG when the app must start with the NAS before Container
Station, must appear in App Center, or must run on a model with too little
RAM for Container Station.

**When NOT to apply.** When the task is modifying an existing native vendor
package, the choice is already made; see QPKG-035 instead.

## QPKG-002 — Set `QPKG_NAME`, `QPKG_VER` and `QPKG_AUTHOR` with no whitespace

**What.** Every `qpkg.cfg` sets `QPKG_NAME` (at most 20 characters),
`QPKG_VER` (at most 10 characters, dotted numeric such as `1.4.2`) and
`QPKG_AUTHOR`. None of them contains whitespace.

**Why.** `qbuild` refuses to build without them. A value with a space is
silently cut at the first space with only a warning (QDK guide §5). The
package's 100-byte binary tail stores the version in a 10-character field:
QDK 2.5.1 truncated longer versions, which made App Center report updates
such as `0.1.1.2101 -> 0.1.1`, and 2.5.2 reverted that. The QDK helpers
`is_less` / `is_greater` compare dotted numeric segments, so a version such as
`1.4.2-beta` sorts unpredictably.

**How.**

```sh
# qpkg.cfg
QPKG_NAME="myapp"
QPKG_VER="1.4.2"
QPKG_AUTHOR="example"
QPKG_DISPLAY_NAME="My App"   # free text for the UI belongs here, not in QPKG_NAME
```

**When NOT to apply.** Never. These fields are the package's identity in
`qpkg.conf` and App Center.

## QPKG-003 — Build with `qbuild --strict`

**What.** Release and CI builds run `qbuild --strict` (or set
`QDK_STRICT=TRUE` in `qdk.conf` or the environment), so every `qbuild`
warning fails the build.

**Why.** Without strict mode, real defects are warnings that scroll past: a
missing `QPKG_SERVICE_PROGRAM`, a truncated name or version (QPKG-002), or a
`QPKG_CONFIG` file missing from the tree. The package builds and only fails
later on a NAS (QDK guide §5, §9).

**How.**

```sh
qbuild --strict --build-dir build
```

**When NOT to apply.** Local throwaway builds while scaffolding may skip it.
Keep it on for anything a user installs.

---

## QPKG-004 — Put shared files in `shared/` and keep only the arch dirs you ship

**What.** Files the same on every architecture go in `shared/`. An
architecture directory (`x86_64`, `arm_64` for aarch64, `arm-x41` for Annapurna
AL-314 armv7) holds only that architecture's binaries and overrides. Delete
every architecture directory you do not build for.

**Why.** `qbuild` builds one package for each non-empty architecture
directory, and files there override `shared/`. A stray file in an unused
directory produces a package for a platform you never tested. The armv7
names are easy to confuse: in `qbuild`, `arm-x31` rejects `ARM_AL` (it is the
Mindspeed line) and `arm-x41` rejects `ARM_MS` (it is Annapurna AL-314). A
package built for the wrong one is refused at install with "Wrong
architecture". The QDK guide (§13) lists `arm-x19`, `arm-x31` and
`x86_ce53xx` as unsupported, although `qbuild` still accepts them.

**How.**

```text
myapp/
├── qpkg.cfg
├── package_routines
├── shared/        # myapp.sh service script, config templates, web assets
├── x86_64/        # bin/myapp built for x86_64
└── arm_64/        # bin/myapp built for aarch64
```

**When NOT to apply.** A pure-script package with no native code needs no
architecture directory: with none populated, `qbuild` makes one
architecture-less package from `shared/` (QDK guide §13).

## QPKG-005 — Set `QTS_MINI_VERSION`; set `QTS_MAX_VERSION` only for a known break

**What.** `qpkg.cfg` sets `QTS_MINI_VERSION` to the oldest firmware you have
tested. Set `QTS_MAX_VERSION` only when a specific newer firmware is known to
break the package.

**Why.** The installer compares these against the running firmware (from
`/etc/default_config/uLinux.conf` since QDK 2.5.3) and refuses to install,
with a notification telling the user to upgrade or downgrade. Without a
minimum, the package installs on firmware where it then fails at runtime. A
speculative maximum blocks every user on the next firmware the day it ships,
even when nothing broke. QDK 2.5.1 fixed the comparison to work per segment.

**How.**

```sh
QTS_MINI_VERSION="5.0.0"
# QTS_MAX_VERSION="7.0.0"   # only after confirming a break on 7.0
```

**When NOT to apply.** Never omit the minimum. The maximum is the exception
this rule describes.

## QPKG-006 — Check the built package with `qbuild --query` before release

**What.** CI inspects each built `.qpkg` with `qbuild --query info`,
`--query dump` and `--query require`, and asserts the name, version and
requirements it expects.

**Why.** The values that matter are the ones in the built file's tail and
control archive, not the ones you meant to set in `qpkg.cfg`. A build-time
variable or a stale `build/` tree can ship the wrong version, which App Center
then treats as an upgrade or a downgrade (QDK guide §9).

**How.**

```sh
pkg=build/myapp_1.4.2_x86_64.qpkg
qbuild --query info "$pkg" | grep -q 'myapp' || exit 1
qbuild --query dump "$pkg" | grep -q '^QPKG_VER="1.4.2"' || exit 1
```

**When NOT to apply.** Only in CI. Never run `qbuild --query` or
`--extract` on a package you did not build yourself; see QPKG-036.

## QPKG-007 — Bundle your runtime; never require QNAP's language QPKGs

**What.** Ship the interpreter or runtime your app needs inside the package,
or require Entware. Do not put QNAP's `Python`, `Python3`, `JRE` or `MariaDB`
QPKGs in `QPKG_REQUIRE`, and do not depend on Optware.

**Why.** Optware has been unsupported since QTS 4.2.0 (QDK README). The QTS
6.1.0 Public Beta release notes (2026-10-13) say 6.1.0 no longer supports the
Python, Python3, JRE and MariaDB packages, so a `QPKG_REQUIRE` on them stops
the install. QNAP's own QuObjects ships its own Python 3.11 inside the
package for the same reason.

**How.**

```text
x86_64/python/        # a relocatable interpreter built for the target
shared/myapp.sh       # PATH="$QPKG_ROOT/python/bin:$PATH"
```

A static binary (QPKG-008) avoids the question entirely.

**When NOT to apply.** A package that is an add-on for another QPKG (a plugin
for a specific app) should declare that app in `QPKG_REQUIRE`.
